overview.narrative:
In this course, students work through the technical side of print color: how to measure it, compare it to standards, adjust it, and document it clearly. The class is less about abstract manufacturing theory and more about hands-on control of ink, substrate, proofing, and color-management variables using the tools and workflows common to print production labs.

The first part of the term builds core measurement habits through quizzes, instrument workshops, CMYK sampling, and perception activities. From there, students move into substrate testing, ink formulation, profiling, proof evaluation, and spot-color workflows, with the Brand Color Report serving as the capstone that pulls the semester's separate lab skills into one integrated technical analysis.
at_a_glance: Instrument-heavy course built around spectrophotometers, proofing systems, and lab testing
Frequent short quizzes paired with hands-on labs rather than theory-only coverage
Strong use of Excel templates, charts, graphs, and formal technical reporting
Capstone project accumulates work across the semester instead of appearing only at the end
Emphasis is on measurement, control, and reproduction quality more than on manufacturing-process theory
overview.who_for: Designed for students who have basic print-process familiarity from GC 1040 and are ready to deepen their measurement, color-control, and materials-analysis skills in a lab-based production-science setting.
overview.arc: Students begin with color reproduction basics and measurement practice, move into substrate and ink testing, then build toward profiling, proofing, and an integrated brand-color capstone. By the end, the course shifts from isolated measurements to explaining how multiple variables shape the same target color across outputs.

prereq_gaps: Catalog prerequisite GC 1040 appears to provide broad print-process and file-prep capability, but this course still encounters a gap in process-color combination/halftone understanding when students reach profiling.
The course assumes only basic CMYK identification at entry for early labs, not the catalog's stated 'thorough understanding of color theory, primarily CMYK.'

General software/file-management competence is assumed across Excel templates, Photoshop, Illustrator, and server-based file handling, but only parts of that expectation are named explicitly in the catalog incoming-skills list.
objective_misalignments: Objective 1 overstates delivered outcomes: the course more clearly assesses ink/substrate properties, testing, and printing consequences than manufacturing-process understanding.

Objective 4 partly duplicates incoming expectations in wording: students do not arrive with a 'thorough understanding' of CMYK process color, and the course itself develops deeper process-color understanding during profiling/proofing work.

The materials strongly evidence technical documentation and reporting through SOP-style procedures, Excel analysis, charts/graphs, and formal lab reports, but that reporting outcome is not named explicitly in the catalog objectives.

The materials strongly evidence proofing/profile workflows with ICC and CxF plus ISO control-wedge comparison, which is richer and more operational than the catalog's broader phrasing about characterization data and proofing systems.
cross_source_conflicts: Catalog objective 1 claims students develop understanding of 'the manufacturing processes used to create inks and substrates,' but the instructor states, 'The ink manufacturing process isn't covered explicitly' and graded coverage is only 'some quiz questions.'

Catalog incoming skill 'thorough understanding of color theory, primarily CMYK' is overstated against the instructor's entry picture: 'They generally know what CMYK is,' but 'some of them lack a full understanding of how the colors combine.'

Canvas Module List references 'Paper Manufacturing Video' (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E4C3X26dxbM) in Unit 2, but no fetched transcript/material is present here; likely background on paper manufacturing, so manufacturing-process K/U may be understated slightly.

Lab: Munsell 100 Hue Test references a YouTube video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AJH7rDgTA3E) that was not available as a fetched course material; likely explains the hue-test procedure, so color-perception setup detail is only partially visible.

Multiple classic quizzes and both exams are listed but question text is 'not exposed via API,' so exact tested vocabulary and reasoning coverage inside quizzes/exams cannot be verified from readable evidence.
suggested_objective_revisions: Students will measure printed color, ink, and substrate samples with industry-standard instruments and record results using correct settings, units, and documentation conventions.
Students will calculate and interpret color-difference, tone-value, and related print metrics against standards and tolerances to evaluate reproduction quality.
Students will test substrate and ink properties, analyze correlations among measured results, and explain how those properties affect print behavior.
Students will create and apply ICC- and CxF-based workflows to profile device output, produce proofs, and compare proof results against print standards.
Students will formulate spot inks to target colors, iteratively adjust recipes based on measured results, and document both technical performance and production cost.
Students will synthesize measurement, formulation, substrate, and proofing data in a technical Brand Color Report that evaluates color reproduction across output conditions.

notes: Brand Color Report is built incrementally through the semester, but the visible evidence shows staged accumulation more than an explicit generate-then-consolidate pedagogy.
Ink Formulation requires iterative correction until '∆E00 < 2,' so students do respond to unsuccessful first matches; this supports revision cycles more than open-ended exploration.

The course reaches D4-level proofing/brand-color integration while curiosity is low and grading is 'mainly tied to completing the required workflow' — a mild unproductive-success pattern rather than a discovery-heavy design.

overview.narrative:
In this course, students study color reproduction through the physical behavior of inks, substrates, and proofing systems. The class is less about abstract manufacturing theory and more about measuring, testing, comparing, and controlling print color with the instruments and workflows used in production settings.

The semester is built around labs: students measure Lab values with spectrophotometers, calculate color difference, test substrate and ink properties, build ICC profiles, compare proofs to press samples, and work through spot-color workflows with CxF data. By the end, those strands come together in the Brand Color Report, where students follow one target color across formulation, substrate behavior, process conversion, and proof accuracy.
at_a_glance: Hands-on measurement course built around spectrophotometers, proofing systems, and materials testing
Frequent short quizzes support lecture units, but the deepest learning happens in labs and the capstone
Strong emphasis on Delta E, Lab data, standards, and tolerances rather than purely visual color talk
Students work across both process-color and spot-color workflows, including ICC and CxF paths
Technical documentation matters: reports, charts, graphs, formulas, and labeled samples are part of the work
overview.who_for: Designed for students who already have basic print-process familiarity from GC 1040 and are ready to deepen their technical control of color, materials, and proofing workflows.
overview.arc: Students begin with color reproduction basics and instrumented measurement, move into substrate and ink testing, then build toward profiling, proofing, and a semester-long Brand Color Report that integrates the earlier labs. The back half of the course shifts from isolated measurements toward workflow comparison and reproduction accuracy across outputs.

Students arrive able to identify CMYK solids, but not reliably able to explain how halftones and process-color combinations create target hues; this gap becomes visible in profiling work and is developed here rather than cleanly supplied by prereqs.

The course assumes spreadsheet comfort, file handling, and basic print-process vocabulary across labs and templates, but those operational prerequisites are clearer in assignments than in the stated prerequisite list.
objective_misalignments: Catalog objective 1 overstates manufacturing-process coverage; the stronger evidenced outcome is testing, correlating, and interpreting ink/substrate properties rather than explaining how inks or substrates are manufactured.

Catalog objective 4 positions color theory as prior knowledge, but the instructor indicates this course develops a deeper understanding of CMYK combination behavior and halftone-controlled color during profiling work.

Catalog objective 6 is supported, but the visible evidence shows a broader proofing workflow than 'create accurate proofing systems' alone, including ISO 12647-7 control-wedge comparison and CxF spot-color certification.

Course materials strongly evidence technical documentation outcomes—SOP-style procedures, Excel calculations, labeled graphs, cost calculations, and formal reports—that are not named clearly in the catalog objectives.
cross_source_conflicts: Catalog objective 1 claims understanding of 'the manufacturing processes used to create inks and substrates,' but the instructor states 'The ink manufacturing process isn't covered explicitly' and graded coverage is limited to 'some quiz questions.'

Catalog incoming skill 'thorough understanding of color theory, primarily CMYK' overstates actual entry ability; the instructor reports students 'generally know what CMYK is' but hesitate on how colors combine and show the gap 'when we get to color profiling.'

The Canvas page 'Brand Color Report Instructions' says students will 'thoroughly examine two defined colors,' while the assignment header and rubric describe the capstone in singular terms as examining 'a color.'

Module list references inaccessible or weakly accessible content whose full instructional value could not be verified: 'Paper Manufacturing Video' (YouTube URL in Unit 2), 'Paper Grain Demo Video' in Substrate Properties Testing, multiple classic quizzes with question text not exposed via API, and the file 'Standards and Specifications.m4v'; these likely support lecture/background knowledge and may make K scores slightly conservative.

overview.narrative:
In this course, students learn how printed color behaves in the real world by measuring it, testing the materials that carry it, and judging how accurately it can be reproduced. The class is less about abstract manufacturing theory and more about hands-on color science: spectrophotometers, Delta E, substrate tests, ink formulation, proofing, and standards-based comparison.

The course moves from foundational color measurement into material behavior and then into full color-management workflows. Along the way, students build technical fluency through labs, quizzes, reports, and proofing exercises, then bring everything together in a Brand Color Report that traces one color across formulation, substrates, CMYK/RGB reproduction, and final proof accuracy.
at_a_glance: Strongly hands-on, instrument-driven lab course
Centers on measured color, not just color theory vocabulary
Builds from patch measurement into profiling and proofing
Uses Excel, X-Rite tools, ICC workflows, and CxF spot-color workflows
Capstone report accumulates work across the semester rather than standing alone
Assessment mixes many short quizzes with substantial lab submissions and one major report
overview.who_for: Designed for students who have completed GC 1040 and are ready to move from basic print-process familiarity into measured color, materials testing, and production-quality control workflows.
overview.arc: Students start with color reproduction basics, perception, and instrument practice, then move into substrate and ink testing before shifting into profiling, proofing, and a semester-long Brand Color Report. By the end, the separate labs converge into one integrated color-analysis workflow across materials, process color, and proof output.

prereq_gaps: Catalog prerequisite GC 1040 does not appear to guarantee the catalog's claimed incoming depth in CMYK color theory; the instructor reports students often arrive with only basic CMYK recognition and struggle when profiling requires deeper process-color reasoning.

The course assumes students can identify basic CMYK separations on entry for early labs, but deeper understanding of halftone-controlled color combination is built in GC 3460 rather than reliably delivered beforehand.

General spreadsheet/file-management competence is functionally required by the Excel-based survey, templates, and report assembly, but that operational expectation is more visible in assignments than in the formal prerequisite statement.
objective_misalignments: Objective 1 names "manufacturing processes used to create inks and substrates," but the course evidence supports lecture exposure to ink makeup and background substrate-manufacturing context more than a developed manufacturing-process outcome.
Objective 2 aligns strongly with the materials: multiple labs require testing inks and substrates with industry instruments and recording measured results.
Objective 3 aligns strongly with the materials through CMYK survey, banded-roll metrics, tone value/density work, and standards-based comparison tasks.
Objective 4 is partly misframed as an incoming skill in the catalog but is also developed in the course, especially once students reach profiling and reproduction analysis.
Objective 6 aligns with the profiling/proofing sequence: students create ICC profiles, produce proofs, and compare ISO control-wedge results against print samples.

A delivered outcome not named cleanly in the catalog is technical documentation: rubrics and templates repeatedly require SOP-style procedure writing, labeled charts/graphs, and formal report discussion.
cross_source_conflicts: Catalog objective 1 overstates manufacturing coverage: the instructor says, "The ink manufacturing process isn't covered explicitly," while visible graded work centers on testing, formulation, and analysis rather than manufacturing processes.

Catalog incoming skill claim of a "thorough understanding of color theory, primarily CMYK" is stronger than the instructor's entry-skill description that students "generally know what CMYK is" but often hesitate on how process colors combine.

overview.narrative:
This course introduces students to brand communications through a mix of industry context, strategic frameworks, and project-based campaign work. Rather than treating branding as only message-making, it asks students to connect people, culture, business goals, and creative choices in a way that feels purposeful and current.

The semester is built around team projects. Students first learn how to frame a brand challenge through insight, audience, and creative-brief thinking, then carry that strategy into a larger brand playbook presentation that includes concept direction, tone, assets, media touchpoints, and storytelling. Weekly WARC and AdWeek responses, ANA MarTech training, and portfolio-oriented lab work keep the course tied to industry practice and professional development.
at_a_glance: Foundation course for the Brand Communications minor
Strongly project-based, with team briefs and campaign playbook presentations
Industry platforms like WARC, AdWeek, and ANA are built into weekly work
Heavy emphasis on consumer insight before creative execution
Lab time is used for team breakouts, coaching, and refinement
Professional presentation quality counts, not just the idea itself
overview.who_for: Designed for students entering the Brand Communications minor who want a broad first look at strategy, creativity, teamwork, and the industry tools used across the field.
overview.arc: Students begin by learning the language, roles, and research habits of brand communications, then move into audience insight and creative brief work before building a larger campaign playbook with media, tone, assets, and presentation components. Alongside the main team projects, they keep up with industry readings, martech training, and a personal portfolio thread that connects the course to professional identity.

prereq_gaps: Catalog prerequisite of only 'Sophomore standing' understates the practical need for comfort with ambiguous briefs, team-based work, and basic research habits to succeed in the course's insight-driven projects.
The course appears to assume some exposure to people/culture reasoning from gen eds or intro marketing/communication, but that preparation is not named in the official prerequisite language.
Students are not assumed to arrive with strong business-style presentation skill or teamwork experience; those are developed in the course despite being essential to major assignments.
objective_misalignments: Catalog objective 3 ('Learn and activate a series of marketing-tech tools available to brands to generate communication planning') appears overstated relative to the visible evidence, which centers on structured ANA certificate completion and reflection more than independent martech tool deployment.

Catalog objective 4 foregrounds critical evaluation 'through team collaboration,' but the materials more concretely show students constructing and presenting strategy artifacts than systematically evaluating market campaigns with a formal critique framework.

The materials strongly emphasize consumer insight development, creative brief construction, and translating emotion/culture into campaign strategy, which are more specific than the broad catalog wording about an industry 'overview.'
cross_source_conflicts: Multiple core grading documents are referenced but unreadable in the extracted materials — 'Midterm_Brand Purpose Strategy_Rubric (2).xlsx', 'Brand Playbook_Purpose Campaign_Final Project-summer 2026.docx', 'Final_Brand Playbook_Rubric_sp 26.xlsx', and 'Final_Brand Playbook_Rubric_sp 26.pdf' — likely the main sources for criterion-level scoring on strategy and presentation.

Several Canvas Pages and recordings are visible but not readable as full content, including 'Week 1: Course Kick Off Recording,' 'VIDEO: Creative Briefs & Brand Playbook,' and 'Project Examples - Brand Building Playbook Part 1'; these likely contain modeling and examples that support strategy and presentation instruction.
The Google Sheet team-assignment resource is not shared ('1kRK_s674c6n…'), so direct evidence of team-role setup and team logistics is incomplete.

overview.narrative:
This course introduces students to brand communications as a connected practice rather than a single job function. Students work across strategy, insight, creative planning, media thinking, and introductory martech exposure while using industry-facing tools like WARC, AdWeek, and ANA resources.

The class is heavily project-based. Teams choose or analyze purpose-driven brands, build a creative brief, and then carry that strategy into a larger campaign playbook presentation. Along the way, students practice consumer-insight development, brand storytelling, and professional slide-based communication, while the linked lab asks them to start shaping a personal portfolio they can carry forward in the minor.
at_a_glance: Foundation course for the Brand Communications minor
Strong use of WARC, AdWeek, and ANA materials as industry inputs
Centered on team strategy and presentation work rather than exams
Purpose-driven campaign framing is a recurring through-line
Simulates agency/brand roles through assigned team functions
Includes a linked lab portfolio project alongside the main class
overview.who_for: Designed for students entering the Brand Communications minor who have general sophomore-level academic experience but are still building strategic, collaborative, and industry-style presentation habits.
overview.arc: Students begin with brand purpose, ecosystem roles, and industry tools, then move into consumer insight and creative-brief work before building toward a final campaign playbook with media, message, and presentation layers. overview.narrative:
This course serves as an entry point into brand communications by introducing students to the industry's core strategic and creative building blocks. Students work through purpose-driven brand challenges, using consumer insight, cultural context, and strategic framing to understand how campaigns take shape.

The class is project-based and team-centered. Students build a midterm creative brief, then carry that logic into a final brand playbook that connects audience insight, big idea, brand assets, media journey thinking, and presentation. Industry tools like WARC, AdWeek, and ANA give the course a professional orientation, while the linked lab extends the work into portfolio building and team development.
at_a_glance: Six-week survey course with a linked lab component
Built around a midterm creative brief and a final campaign playbook
Strong use of WARC, AdWeek, and ANA industry platforms
Heavily team-based, with assigned brand-agency style roles
Emphasizes purpose-driven brands, consumer insight, and strategic storytelling
Presentation quality and professional polish materially affect grades
overview.who_for: Designed for students entering the Brand Communications minor who are ready for an overview course that blends industry orientation, team project work, and introductory strategic brand thinking.
overview.arc: Students begin with industry orientation, brand-purpose cases, and team formation, then move into insight and creative-brief work before building out a fuller campaign playbook with media, big-idea, and brand-expression elements. Alongside the team arc, they complete recurring industry-reading responses, ANA MarTech modules, and a linked portfolio build.

overview.narrative:
In this course, students learn how to turn a brand problem into a paid-media recommendation across the major channel types. The semester moves from channel characteristics and planning math into applied planning work in print, out-of-home, broadcast, paid search, paid social, display, and measurement.

The course is hands-on and assignment-driven. Students complete frequent short activities and homework tasks, then bring those pieces together in a final group presentation that asks them to define the business challenge, plan the audience and strategy, allocate budget, and explain why the recommendation should work.
at_a_glance: Structured around weekly channel modules rather than one continuous campaign from day one.
Strong mix of media math, channel evaluation, and client-style recommendation building.
Final project is group-based, but students are individually graded on their own section and question handling.
Revision is built into the course through redo opportunities and workshop-style feedback before the final presentation.
Paid search exposure includes Google Search certification rather than only instructor-made assignments.
overview.who_for: Designed for students who want an applied introduction to paid-media planning and are ready to translate general brand-communications context into channel and budget decisions.
overview.arc: Students start with channel fundamentals and planning math, move through print/OOH, broadcast, paid search/social, and digital display/measurement, then spend the closing weeks building and refining a multi-channel recommendation for a final client presentation.

overview.narrative:
In this course, students learn how to plan paid media across a full channel mix, from traditional formats like print, out-of-home, radio, and TV to digital search, social, display, and measurement. The work is applied rather than abstract: students practice the math, evaluate media options, and learn to justify why a channel or mix makes sense for a given audience and objective.

The course builds toward a group final project that functions like a media-agency recommendation. Students choose from instructor-selected clients, define the business challenge and target audience, build a strategy and budget allocation, and present the recommendation live in class. Along the way, the course uses workshop feedback, revision opportunities, and short written assignments to sharpen both planning judgment and communication.
at_a_glance: Channel-by-channel structure before the integrated final project
Heavy use of worksheets, planning math, and applied in-class activities
Final project simulates agency-style media recommendation work
Students can revise work after feedback for higher grades
Google Search certification adds an external platform credential
Presentation grading includes both deck content and live Q&A
overview.who_for: Designed for students who have general brand-communications background and want practical entry-level media-planning experience without needing prior technical media-buying skills.
overview.arc: Students begin with channel basics and media math, move through print, out-of-home, broadcast, search, social, display, and measurement, then spend the last stretch building and refining a full communications plan for a chosen client. The semester ends with an individually graded group presentation that asks students to explain and defend their recommendations live.

overview.narrative:
In this course, students learn how paid-media plans are built across the major channel types, from print and out-of-home through broadcast, search, social, display, and measurement. The work is applied and planning-oriented: students practice the math, evaluate example plans and buys, and gradually build toward making their own recommendations.

The course is organized like a guided media-planning sequence rather than a theory survey alone. Early weeks break the work into channel modules and structured activities; later weeks shift into communications planning and workshop time for the final project. The semester culminates in a client-style group presentation where students present a full recommendation and answer questions on their section.
at_a_glance: Channel-by-channel structure before the integrated final plan
Frequent worksheets and class activities on media math and plan evaluation
Strong paid-media focus across both traditional and digital channels
Group final project with individual grading during the live presentation
Workshop-style feedback in the final weeks rather than a one-shot project submission
Google Search certification included as a course component
overview.who_for: Designed for students entering paid-media or communications-planning work who need structured practice turning channel knowledge into recommendation-ready plans.
overview.arc: Students start with channel fundamentals and media math, move through print, outdoor, broadcast, search, social, and digital display, then spend the back third of the semester building a full communications channel plan for a selected client. The semester ends with a group presentation where each student explains and defends their part of the recommendation.

overview.narrative:
GC 3460 explores how inks, substrates, and output systems affect printed color. Students work with measurement instruments, test material properties, and use color-difference calculations to compare samples with standards and targets.

The course combines lectures, quizzes, exams, and practical labs. Students formulate and correct inks, create color profiles, and evaluate proofs, then bring their work together in a Brand Color Report that follows color from its definition through reproduction across multiple outputs.
at_a_glance: Lecture-and-lab production-science format
Hands-on spectrophotometric measurement
Software-supported ink correction to a numerical tolerance
ICC and CxF proofing workflows
Incremental Brand Color Report capstone
Technical reports alongside quizzes and exams
overview.who_for: Designed for Graphic Communications students who have completed GC 1040 and are ready to connect print-production experience with color and materials testing.
overview.arc: Students begin with color reproduction and measurement, move into single-color and substrate testing, and then develop profiling and proofing workflows. The Brand Color Report brings these strands together incrementally across the semester.

overview.narrative:
GC 3460 explores what it takes to reproduce color reliably with different inks, substrates, and output systems. Students work with printed samples, measurement instruments, and industry software to test materials, compare color targets, and examine the behavior of printing processes.

Laboratory work moves from spectrophotometer measurements and substrate testing into ink formulation, press profiling, and proof evaluation. A semester-long Brand Color Report brings these activities together through physical samples, color-accuracy comparisons, labeled data displays, and technical discussion.

Instrumented testing of real printed samples and materials
Software-guided ink correction to a numerical tolerance
ICC and CxF workflows connected to physical proof output
Semester-long Brand Color Report
Technical reports alongside quizzes and exams

overview.narrative:
GC 3460 explores how inks, substrates, and output systems shape printed color. Students measure color and material properties, compare results with targets, and use laboratory data to understand differences in print reproduction.

The course combines guided laboratory workflows with technical reporting. Students formulate and correct inks, characterize press output with ICC profiles, and evaluate proofs through visual and measured comparisons. A staged Brand Color Report connects these activities through the challenge of reproducing a defined color across materials and output systems.

Instrumented measurement with X-Rite and Techkon equipment
Iterative ink matching with X-Rite Autura
ICC and CxF proofing workflows
Semester-long Brand Color Report
Technical reports alongside quizzes and exams

Survey of Brand Communications introduces students to the strategic and creative work behind purpose-driven brand campaigns. Working in teams, students investigate consumers, connect people and culture to a brand opportunity, and turn that research into a creative brief.

overview.narrative:
In this course, students explore how brands connect with people through consumer insight, cultural understanding, creative strategy, and media choices. Working in teams, they research a brand and build a creative brief that becomes the foundation for an integrated campaign recommendation.

The emphasis is on making thoughtful connections: why an audience cares, what a brand can credibly offer, and how a creative idea carries that relationship into messaging and channels. Teams refine their work through coaching and present it with the organization, visual clarity, and coordinated delivery expected in a brand-team setting.
at_a_glance: Broad introduction to creative strategy rather than advanced production specialization
Team roles modeled on brand and agency practice
One-page strategic brief leading into an integrated campaign recommendation
Draft coaching and team breakouts before final presentation
AI used to support insight work and concept representation
Professional presentation expectations, including coordinated delivery and careful visual organization

overview.narrative:
Survey of Brand Communications introduces students to the strategic and creative work behind purpose-driven brand campaigns. Working in teams, students connect audience motivations, cultural context, and brand capabilities to a communication opportunity, then shape that opportunity into a creative brief.

The brief becomes the foundation for a campaign playbook incorporating a big idea, brand assets, emotional tone, creative concepts, and a basic media plan. Team discussions and instructor coaching help students move beyond surface observations toward stronger insights. Presentations emphasize a clear strategic story, thoughtful visuals, and credible delivery.
at_a_glance: Broad introductory coverage rather than specialist production training
Role-based team projects
One-page strategic brief leading into a final campaign playbook
Draft coaching and team breakouts before final presentations
AI used to support research and concept representation
Strong emphasis on professional presentation credibility

The course culminates in a group client recommendation developed through workshops and delivered as a presentation, with each student responsible for explaining their section and answering questions.

overview.narrative:
Media Management in Brand Communications introduces students to paid-media planning across print, out-of-home, broadcast, search, social, and digital display. Through calculations, channel evaluations, and planning exercises, students learn to connect media choices to audiences and campaign objectives rather than personal preference.

The course culminates in a group recommendation for a selected client. Students define the planning problem, develop channel strategy and budget allocation, propose measurement, and present their reasoning in class. Formula-supported mathematics and opportunities to revise work make the course accessible while building practical planning habits.
at_a_glance: Traditional and digital channels taught in a sequential weekly structure
Media mathematics taught from scratch with formulas supplied
Frequent worksheets, discussions, and small-group activities
Google Search certification included
Final-project workshops provide continuing feedback
Group presentation with individual explanation and question handling graded
overview.who_for: Designed for students developing a foundation in paid-media planning, with GC 3700 recommended as brand-communications preparation.
overview.arc: Students begin with media types and planning mathematics, move through traditional and digital channel planning, then bring those pieces together in a client-focused recommendation and final presentation.

overview.narrative:
Media Management in Brand Communications introduces students to the decisions behind a paid-media recommendation: which channels to use, how to allocate a budget, and how to assess success. Traditional and digital media work leads into a group project that connects a client's business challenge with an audience, campaign objective, and channel strategy.

The course combines planning exercises with feedback and revision. Media math is taught from scratch with formulas provided, and students can rethink incorrect answers and resubmit work. In the final weeks, groups workshop their recommendations before presenting in class; each student is assessed on explaining their section and answering questions.

Media math taught from scratch with formulas supplied
Opportunities to resubmit work after targeted feedback
Student-selected planning decisions within a supplied client list
Final group presentation with individual assessment

overview.arc: Students move through traditional and digital media planning before bringing those tools into a client-focused communications plan. The closing weeks are workshops for refining the recommendation, followed by an in-person group presentation.
